extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners (USPTO); patent practitioners as secondary audience
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claim subject matter is a judicial exception under 35 U.S.C. § 101 (abstract ideas, mental processes, laws/natural phenomena, products of nature) and procedures for examiners when applying the eligibility framework (Steps 2A/2B, pathways, TC Director approval).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial or Legal Interactions (abstract idea grouping)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Commercial interactions” or “legal interactions” include agreements in the form of contracts, legal obligations, advertising, marketing or sales activities or behaviors, and business relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims reciting commercial/legal interactions are often directed to abstract ideas. Example: buySAFE (transaction performance guaranty — creating a contractual relationship was found to be an abstract idea). Other examples include managing a stable value protected life insurance policy (Bancorp), processing insurance claims under an insurance policy (Accenture), tax-free real estate exchanges (Fort Properties), hedging (Bilski), mitigating settlement risk (Alice), arbitration (In re Comiskey), using advertising as an exchange/currency (Ultramercial), structuring a sales force or marketing company (In re Ferguson), algorithms for visit optimization (In re Maucorps), offer-based price optimization (OIP Techs. v. Amazon), processing applications through a dealer/bank clearing-house (Dealertrack), and processing applications for financing (Credit Acceptance). Examiner guidance: treat such claims as within the “methods of organizing human activity”/abstract idea grouping when appropriate and analyze under the subject matter eligibility framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing personal behavior/relationships/interactions between people (organizing human activity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sub-grouping “managing personal behavior or relationships or interactions between people” includes social activities, teaching, and following rules or instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that organize human activity in these ways have been treated as abstract ideas. Examples: storing user-selected preset spending limits and notifying users (budgeting) — Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One (tracked as abstract idea of tracking transactions against limits); filtering content (BASCOM), considering historical usage while inputting data (BSG Tech. v. Buyseasons), mental processes used by a neurologist testing a patient (In re Meyer), voting/self-verifying ballots (Voter Verified), attention manager for providing information without disrupting primary activity (Interval Licensing v. AOL), following game rules (In re Marco Guldenaar — dice game), assigning hair designs to balance head shape (In re Brown), and hedging instructions (Bilski). Examiner guidance: identify whether the claim is directed to these types of human-activity organization concepts when performing the §101 analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental Processes — general rule (abstract idea grouping)
rubrics_metrics.description: The courts consider a mental process (thinking) that “can be performed in the human mind, or by a human using a pen and paper” to be an abstract idea. Mental processes include observations, evaluations, judgments, and opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authoritative citations: CyberSource, Benson, Mayo, Parker v. Flook. Examiners should recognize that methods which can be performed mentally or with simple physical aids are ‘basic tools’ and are unpatentable abstract ideas. When a claim’s limitations are of the nature of mental processes (observations, evaluations, judgments, opinions) and are recited at a high level of generality, treat them as abstract ideas and proceed with the eligibility framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental Processes — A: Limitations that cannot practically be performed in the human mind are not mental processes
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim with limitation(s) that cannot practically be performed in the human mind does not recite a mental process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the human mind is not equipped to perform the claimed limitation(s), the claim may not fall in the mental-process grouping. Examples of claims not reciting mental processes: GPS receiver calculating pseudoranges to estimate distance and time (SiRF Tech.), detecting suspicious activity using network monitors and analyzing network packets (SRI Int’l), a specific multi-step data encryption method involving manipulation of data structures (Synopsys), and rendering a halftone image by pixel-by-pixel comparison against a blue noise mask that outputs a modified computer data structure (Research Corp. Techs.). Examiner guidance: evaluate whether the claim limitations could practically be performed mentally; if not, do not treat them as mental-process abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental Processes — B: Claims that encompass human performance mentally (with or without physical aid) recite mental processes
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that encompasses a human performing the step(s) mentally, with or without a physical aid (e.g., pen and paper), recites a mental process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specification and claim language to determine whether claimed steps are performable mentally. The use of physical aids (pencil/paper, slide rule) does not negate the mental nature — it only accounts for memory/capacity variation. Examples: constructing a map of credit card numbers that can be made by writing down transactions (CyberSource); computations performable by pencil and paper (Flook). Examiner guidance: if a limitation can practically be performed by a person mentally or with simple aids, treat it as a mental-process abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental Processes — C: Claims that require/mention a computer may still recite a mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that require a computer may nonetheless recite a mental process depending on how the claim/specification recites the concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must carefully interpret the claim and specification to determine if the invention is merely a concept performed on a generic computer, performed in a computer environment but analogous to human cognitive actions, or merely using a computer as a tool to perform a mental process. Sub-categories and examples: 1) Performing a mental process on a generic computer — Voter Verified, Versata (claims directed to determining price were abstract despite use of general-purpose hardware). 2) Performing a mental process in a computer environment — Symantec (electronic post office analogized to human mail handling), FairWarning (rules-based detection of misuse analogous to human fraud detection). 3) Using a computer as a tool to perform a mental process — Mortgage Grader (anonymous loan shopping concept could be performed by humans), Berkheimer (parsing/comparing data at high level). Examiner guidance: review specification to see if applicant is claiming a human-mental concept merely performed on computers; if so, treat as a mental process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental Processes — D: Both product and process claims may recite mental processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Both product claims (e.g., computer system, computer-readable medium) and process claims may recite mental processes; the classification depends on the substance of the claimed concept, not the statutory category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of product claims found to recite mental-process-type abstract ideas include: APIs for extracting/processing information from hard copy documents (Content Extraction), computer systems for anonymous loan shopping (Mortgage Grader), computer-readable media for detecting fraud (CyberSource), electronic post offices (Symantec), wide-area real-time electric grid monitoring (Electric Power Group), and storage media implementing pricing methods (Versata). Examiner guidance: do not assume a system or medium claim inherently avoids the mental-process grouping; analyze the underlying concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tentative abstract ideas — examiner procedure and TC Director approval requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A “tentative abstract idea” refers to claim limitations that an examiner believes should be treated as an abstract idea even though they do not fall within the enumerated groupings (mathematical concepts, methods of organizing human activity, mental processes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: 1) If the claim as a whole integrates the tentative abstract idea into a practical application → claim is not directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: NO) → eligible at Pathway B. 2) If the claim as a whole does not integrate into a practical application → claim is directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: YES) → proceed to Step 2B. At Step 2B, if the claim provides an inventive concept (Step 2B: YES) → eligible at Pathway C. 3) If the claim does not provide an inventive concept (Step 2B: NO) → bring application to the Technology Center (TC) director; a rejection of a claim reciting a tentative abstract idea must be approved by the TC director (approval to be indicated in the file record). Office action must identify the previously non-enumerated abstract idea via form paragraph 7.05.017 and include the TC Director’s signature. Examiner guidance: interviews may help; examiner may withdraw or maintain rejection upon considering applicant’s reply; TC Director approval is required only for issuing such a Step 2B rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of Nature, Natural Phenomena & Products of Nature (judicial exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws of nature and natural phenomena include naturally occurring principles/relations and nature-based products that are naturally occurring or that do not have markedly different characteristics compared to what occurs in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categories are judicial exceptions because the manifestations of laws of nature and natural phenomena are ‘‘part of the storehouse of knowledge’’ and not patentable. Examples identified by the courts include: isolated DNA (Myriad), a cloned farm animal (In re Roslin), correlations between DNA regions (Genetic Techs. v. Merial), metabolic correlations (Mayo), correlation of myeloperoxidase and cardiovascular risk (Cleveland Clinic), electromagnetism to transmit signals (O’Reilly v. Morse), bacterial qualities (Funk Bros.), single-stranded primers (Ambry Genetics), chemical principles underlying union of fatty elements and water (Tilghman v. Proctor), existence of cell-free fetal DNA (Ariosa), and genotype–drug risk correlations (Vanda). Examiner guidance: treat such claims as judicial exceptions and apply the subject matter eligibility framework to determine whether additional claim elements integrate the judicial exception into a patent-eligible application.
